runs.analysis:
The stage should narrow the list by separating the few truly vital documents from supporting ones. Selection keeps all Critical, then adds High, Medium and Low only until at least 5 are kept.

Candidate A rates 5 Critical and 8 High, and only 2 Medium. Under the selection rule, 13 of 15 documents are kept, so the filter barely narrows anything. A's own rationales call many High documents "supporting refinement rather than a gate", which makes the ratings feel inflated. Its summary also miscalculates: it says "62%" Critical or High when 13 of 15 is about 87%. Its 80/20 discussion concedes it did not discriminate. The rationales are detailed and well grounded in the plan, and the Critical picks are defensible (geotechnical, oceanographic, rail gauge, cost benchmarks, IMO). But the output does not do the job the stage exists for.

Candidate B rates 1 Critical (ID 0), 2 High (IDs 4 and 13), 7 Medium and 5 Low. Under the selection rule, that keeps 3, then adds Medium to reach 10 documents, dropping the 5 Low ones. That is real prioritization tied to the initial phase. Some ratings are debatable. Rail gauge as Medium is justified by rail being Phase 2. Cost benchmarks as Low and oceanographic data as Medium are arguable, since the plan flags both as gaps. B's summary is a bit loose about which documents are "vital". Even so, B's rationales are specific, cite the plan's issues, and stay internally consistent with the phasing logic.

B fits the stage's purpose better and is more useful downstream, because it narrows the list and makes sensible trade-offs. A's more thorough rationales do not make up for the lack of narrowing.

Selection effect: the code keeps all Critical documents, then adds High, Medium and Low until at least 5 are kept. A has 1 Critical and 2 High, so the 7 Medium documents are also pulled in and 10 of 15 are kept, which barely narrows the list. B has 5 Critical (IDs 0, 2, 6, 9, 11), so exactly 5 are kept. That is a real narrowing, and the set is plausible: seismic and geotechnical data, IMO regulations, rail gauge and interoperability, cost benchmarks and oceanographic data. Rating quality: A is more discriminating and consistent, but some calls are debatable. Oceanographic data is rated Medium and cost benchmarks Low, both questionable for a €40B project at 100 m depth in the Strait. B inflates its ratings, with 13 of 15 High or Critical, and its summary misstates the share as 62% when it is about 87%. B's Critical rationales are well grounded in plan specifics such as lever IDs, risk numbers and cost-overrun precedents. B's output is closer to the stage's purpose of narrowing the list, despite its flaws.

Both candidates produce the same final kept set under the selection rule (8 of 10 documents, excluding ids 5 and 7), so the comparison rests on rationale and summary quality. A's summary claims four Critical and four High, but its own ratings show 3 Critical and 5 High. It also rates the grid/RTE document only High while calling it a "vital few" item. B's ratings and summary are internally consistent (4 Critical, 4 High, 2 Medium). B rates the RTE/grid framework as Critical, which fits the plan's top risk. Its rationales are more specific, citing particular decisions, risks, assumptions and figures. B is verbose and has a stray quote character in its summary, but these flaws are minor next to A's inconsistency.

Both candidates produce the same final selection. The code keeps all Critical documents and, because fewer than 5 are Critical, adds all High ones. That gives ids 0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9 in both cases, so downstream output is identical. The comparison therefore rests on rating quality and internal consistency.

Candidate A rates the RTE/Enedis grid-interconnection document Critical. For a 9 GW grid-dominated project that is the right call. Its counts are internally consistent: 4 Critical, 4 High and 2 Medium, and the summary says exactly that. Its rationales are detailed and tied to the plan's decisions, risks and assumptions. They are verbose, and a few claims overreach, such as saying the document "IS that formal agreement's source" and quoting a hardware cost figure. Even so, they are decision-useful.

Candidate B rates the grid-financing document only High, yet its summary names it among the "absolute vital few". That contradicts its own rating. B's summary also says four documents are Critical and four High, but its list has 3 Critical and 5 High. The rationales are concise and reasonable. They are less specific, and B understates grid risk, which is the main feasibility question in the prompt.

A is more consistent and better prioritised, and its rationales are richer. B is tighter but has factual and logical inconsistencies in the summary.

Selection effect: the stage keeps all Critical documents, then adds High ones if fewer than 5 are Critical. Both candidates have fewer than 5 Critical, so High documents are added. A keeps 7 of 9 (Critical 0, 1, 4; High 2, 3, 5, 6) and drops 7 and 8 as Medium. B keeps 8 of 9 (Critical 0, 1, 4, 5; High 3, 6, 7, 8) and drops only 2.

Ratings against the plan: A's ratings follow the plan's phasing. Reduction cards (id 8) are deferred to a 30-month grace period, so Medium is sensible, and A explains that the T+5 latency benchmark (id 7) can proceed in parallel with the provisional standard. B rates id 8 High and says "required immediately" while its own rationale admits the work is deferred, which is inconsistent. B rates id 5 (cost-attribution policies) Critical, which looks inflated next to the legal text and OSDM spec. B's demotion of id 2 to Medium is defensible but arguable.

Internal consistency: B's summary says "3 out of 9" are High when it rated 4. It also puts id 8 in the Critical "equity floors" cluster although it rated it High. B's summary is thin on explanation. A's summary matches its ratings (3 Critical, 4 High, 2 Medium). It has a stray trailing quote character and is verbose, but its rationales tie each document to specific decisions, risks and assumptions.

Usefulness: A discriminates more sharply, filters out the deferred and secondary documents, and its summary is accurate. B has the counting error and some rating inflation. A is moderately better.

Both candidates keep several documents (A keeps 8 of 9, B keeps 7 of 9). B's ratings follow the plan's critical path more closely: it rates governance precedent (id 2) High, and it rates the deferred reduction-card work (id 8) and the latency benchmarks (id 7) Medium. A rates the cost-attribution document (id 5) Critical and the deferred reduction-card document (id 8) High, and it rates governance precedent (id 2) Medium, which is hard to justify given the plan's governance and stakeholder-resistance risks. A's summary miscounts its own ratings ("High 3 out of 9" when it has 4) and calls ids 4 and 8 "mandatory equity floors" in a Critical grouping, but id 8 is rated High. B's summary counts match its ratings, apart from a stray trailing quote. B's rationales tie each document to specific decisions, risks and assumptions in the plan, though they are verbose.

Candidate A rates only ids 0–6 and never mentions id 7, so it omits a document (the heat-illness escalation/triage script, which B shows exists). Candidate B rates all 8 documents. A rates everything Critical or High, which gives the selection step little to work with. B spreads its ratings across Critical, High, Medium and Low, and ties them to the initial mobilization phase and the Month 2 and Month 4 gates. Some of B's ratings can be argued: id 4 is arguably Critical, and the baseline data at Medium is debatable but defensible. A's rationales are more detailed but verbose, and its summary ends with a stray quote. Overall B is more complete and better calibrated.

A covers all 8 documents (ids 0–7) but its summary contradicts its own ratings. The summary claims 5 Critical, 1 Medium and 0 Low, while A actually gave 4 Critical, 1 Medium and 1 Low. A also rates the baseline mortality/morbidity document as only Medium. That is questionable, because the prompt requires baselines and a measurement plan, and the effect cannot be shown without them. B has more detailed rationales grounded in the plan (Leipzig, the threshold deadline, the Month 1 assessments, the gate metrics). Its ratings are better calibrated, its summary matches its ratings, and it gives a concrete action sequence. B's weaknesses are that it appears to omit id 7, which A rated Critical, that it rates doc 6 High while quoting that the related decision is Medium, and that it is very verbose with a stray quote character at the end of the summary. Overall B is slightly better, though the missing document is a real risk.
